title: Depth-first search and cycles
summary: Go deep before going wide, count connected pieces, and spot cycles with three colours.

steps.title: Go deep first
body: **Depth-first search** (DFS) follows one path as far as it can, then backs up to the last fork and tries the next branch. Recursion does the backing up for you.
From 0, DFS goes to 1, then 1's unvisited neighbour 3, then 3's first unvisited neighbour 2. 2 is a dead end (0 and 3 are visited), so it backs up to 3 and goes on to 4.
Like BFS it is `O(V + E)`. It does not find shortest paths, but it is the natural tool for "explore everything reachable" and for cycles.

steps.prompt: DFS from 0 on the graph from the BFS lesson (BFS gave `0 3 1 4 2 5`). What does DFS print?
steps.explain: DFS dives: 0, 3 (0's first neighbour), 4, 5, then 5's unvisited neighbour 2, then 2's neighbour 1. The graph is one big loop, and DFS walks round it.

steps.title: Connected components
body: An undirected graph may fall into separate pieces, called **connected components**. To count them, loop over every vertex; whenever you find one not yet seen, that is a new component, and a DFS from it marks the whole piece.
Each vertex is visited once overall, so this is still `O(V + E)`. Islands on a map, friend groups, and "which machines can reach each other" are all component questions.

steps.prompt: Complete the iterative DFS that marks one component, using an explicit stack instead of recursion.
steps.explain: Swap BFS's queue for a stack and you get a depth-first order. An explicit stack also avoids stack overflow on very deep graphs.

steps.title: Cycles in directed graphs
body: In a **directed** graph, a cycle is a path that leads back to where it started: `A -> B -> C -> A`. Task dependencies with a cycle can never be scheduled.
DFS finds them with three colours:
- **gray**: on the current DFS path (entered, not finished),
- **black**: finished; everything reachable from it is explored.

Reaching a **gray** vertex means you walked back onto your own path: a cycle. Reaching a black one is fine; it was explored down a different branch. Watch `color` in the trace: vertex 0 is still gray when 2 points back at it.

code: var graph = new List<int>[] { new() { 1 }, new() { 2 }, new() { 0 }, new() { 2 } };

steps.prompt: Edges `0 -> 1`, `0 -> 2`, `1 -> 2`. DFS from 0 finishes 1 and 2, then looks at the edge `0 -> 2` and finds 2 **black**. Is there a cycle?
options: No: 2 is finished and not on the current path
Yes: any edge to a visited vertex is a cycle
steps.explain: Two routes into the same vertex (a diamond) is not a cycle. Only an edge back to a **gray** vertex closes a loop. That is why a simple visited flag is not enough in directed graphs.

steps.prompt: Does each **directed** graph contain a cycle?

steps.title: Count components
prompt: Write `int CountComponents(int n, int[][] edges)` for an **undirected** graph with vertices `0..n-1`. A vertex with no edges is a component on its own.
solution: for (var v = 0; v < n; v++) graph[v] = new List<int>();
foreach (var e in edges) { graph[e[0]].Add(e[1]); graph[e[1]].Add(e[0]); }
template: Dojo.Eq("two components", 2, CountComponents(5, new[] { new[] { 0, 1 }, new[] { 1, 2 }, new[] { 3, 4 } }));
Dojo.Eq("no edges: every vertex alone", 4, CountComponents(4, new int[0][]));
Dojo.Eq("one big cycle", 1, CountComponents(3, new[] { new[] { 0, 1 }, new[] { 1, 2 }, new[] { 2, 0 } }));
Dojo.Eq("isolated vertex counts", 3, CountComponents(5, new[] { new[] { 0, 1 }, new[] { 2, 3 } }));
var dojoEdges = Enumerable.Range(0, 9_999).Where(i => i % 100 != 99).Select(i => new[] { i, i + 1 }).ToArray();
Dojo.Eq("10,000 vertices in 100 chains", 100, CountComponents(10_000, dojoEdges));
hints: Build the adjacency list, then loop over every vertex. An unseen vertex starts a new component.
From each new start, run a DFS (recursive or with a stack) that marks everything it reaches.

steps.title: Detect a cycle
prompt: Write `bool HasCycle(List<int>[] graph)` for a **directed** graph (`graph[v]` lists the vertices `v` points to). Use the white/gray/black colouring, and start a DFS from every white vertex so disconnected parts are checked too.
starter: var color = new int[graph.Length]; // 0 white, 1 gray, 2 black
template: List<int>[] DojoGraph(int n, params (int From, int To)[] edges) { var g = new List<int>[n]; for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) g[i] = new(); foreach (var (f, t) in edges) g[f].Add(t); return g; }
Dojo.Eq("0->1->2->0 has a cycle", true, HasCycle(DojoGraph(3, (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0))));
Dojo.Eq("a diamond has no cycle", false, HasCycle(DojoGraph(4, (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3))));
Dojo.Eq("a self-loop is a cycle", true, HasCycle(DojoGraph(2, (0, 1), (1, 1))));
Dojo.Eq("a cycle in a part not reachable from 0", true, HasCycle(DojoGraph(5, (0, 1), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 2))));
Dojo.Eq("edges into finished vertices are fine", false, HasCycle(DojoGraph(4, (1, 0), (2, 0), (3, 1), (3, 2))));

A gray neighbour means a cycle; a white neighbour needs visiting; a black one is ignored.
